summary: The fourth MIME document. It specifies registration procedures for MIME facilities with IANA, such as media types. It is a best current practice, and it was replaced by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2048 describes how to register MIME media types and other MIME values with IANA. Different types of registration follow different review and approval procedures.

subtitle: The registration rules RFC 2048 defined for MIME media types and related values.

tldr.problem: MIME can accommodate new media types and related values, so participants need a public process for naming and documenting them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns IANA a registry role and defines different procedures for IETF, vendor and personal media-type trees, external-body access types and transfer encodings.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2048 obsoleted RFCs 1521, 1522 and 1590. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289 and updated by RFC 3023.

today: RFC 2048 is a Best Current Practice that obsoleted RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289, and updated by RFC 3023.

sections.title: Why MIME Values Need a Registry
sections.content:
MIME is designed to accept additional object types, character sets and access methods without changing its basic protocol. RFC 2048 defines public registration procedures for media types, external-body access types and content-transfer-encodings.

The RFC assigns IANA a central role in maintaining these registrations. Character-set registration is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME can be extended with new content types and related values. A registry gives participants a shared place to find their names and specifications.

sections.title: Media-Type Registration Trees
sections.content:
The IETF tree is for types of general interest and requires IESG approval and an RFC. The vendor tree uses the vnd. prefix for types associated with commercial products, while the personal tree uses prs. for experimental or non-commercial types.

The x. tree is for unregistered experimental types that parties agree to exchange. The RFC discourages this approach because vendor and personal registrations have simpler procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Media types use different registration paths depending on who owns or needs them. The IETF path requires formal approval, while vendor and personal types can use simpler paths.

sections.title: What a Registration Must Describe
sections.content:
A media type must represent an actual media format, not a transfer encoding or character set. Its type and subtype names must be valid, and all registered types must use one canonical data format.

IETF-tree registrations require a precise, openly available format specification and a security analysis. Vendor and personal registrations have different specification requirements, but the RFC says known security risks must be described accurately for all trees.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration needs a clear name and a description of the format. It must also state known security risks without claiming that unexamined risks do not exist.

sections.title: Review, Changes and Other Registries
sections.content:
The media-type review procedure includes a two-week community review. IETF-tree types also require IESG approval; vendor and personal types may be submitted directly to IANA if they meet the RFC's conditions. A registered type cannot be deleted, but its intended-use field can be changed to OBSOLETE.

External-body access types are reviewed by an appointed reviewer after community review and must be described in an RFC. A new transfer encoding requires a standards-track RFC, a complete algorithm description and justification; the RFC discourages creating many encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: Some types receive community and IESG review before IANA registers them. Other values have their own procedures, and a media type is marked obsolete rather than removed.
